entities.summary:
Galician (Galego) is a Western Romance language closely related to Portuguese, spoken by approximately 2.4 million people primarily in Galicia, the autonomous community of northwestern Spain. Often described as a dialect continuum with Portuguese — the two languages diverged after the 12th-century separation of Portugal from Galicia-León — Galician retains a distinct identity as the indigenous language of one of Spain's most culturally particular regions.

Medieval Galician-Portuguese (11th–14th centuries) was a prestige literary language across the entire Iberian Peninsula — the language of troubadour lyric poetry (cantigas), including Alfonso X of Castile's Cantigas de Santa María. The split between Galician and Portuguese occurred after the Portuguese kingdom consolidated its separate identity; northern Galician became politically subordinate to Castilian Spain while southern Galician evolved into Portuguese. The Rexurdimento (Galician Renaissance, 19th century) — led by Rosalía de Castro, Eduardo Pondal, and Manuel Curros Enríquez — revived Galician literary culture after centuries of subordination to Castilian.

Franco's dictatorship (1939–1975) suppressed Galician as it did Catalan and Basque, relegating it to private speech. The 1978 Spanish constitution and the 1981 Statute of Autonomy of Galicia recognized Galician as co-official with Spanish in Galicia. Today Galician faces demographic decline as younger generations shift to Spanish, despite co-official status and regional language promotion policies — a fate shared by most minority Romance languages in the 21st century.
